# Tesla, Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Reduce
Composite score: 4.0
Data as of: 2026-10-29

## 5分钟速读 Executive Briefing

TSLA closed at $403.30 on 2026-10-29, a $1,594.1B market capitalisation and a $1,558.0B enterprise value, 19% below its 52-week high of $498.83 and 36% above the low of $297.38. The stock is up 14.3% in a month and 30.6% in three, but down 11.3% year to date and 8.4% over twelve months, and the Q3 2026 results on 2026-10-21 — revenue $28.046B, adjusted EPS $0.48 against a $0.45 consensus — have been bought. The regime frames the call: the S&P 500 sits at 7,720.39, up 12.8% year to date and 1.6% below its high, the VIX is 17.20 at the 52nd percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%, up 0.93 points in twelve months, a discount rate that penalises cash flows arriving after 2030. [S15, S141, S22, S23, S24]

### Reduce, at a fraction of the size

Tesla's vehicles, energy and services businesses are worth $43.00 a share on 3,952.6M shares; the remaining $360.30 of the $403.30 price — $1,424B, or 89% of the equity — is an option on robotaxi and robotics that discloses no revenue. Our probability-weighted value is $111, 72% below the close, on a base that carries $259B of autonomy across four weighted branches rather than the $40B regional fleet alone; even a 40% chance of a premium SpaceX exchange lifts expected value only to $248. The action is to trim rather than to sell short: the option has real value, the balance sheet is not the constraint, and a negotiated exchange ratio could pay $443-464 without any operating delivery. [S6, S15, S120]

Confidence is high on the reported numbers — three years of filings, a third quarter reconciled line by line, and a timestamped market price — medium on the 11-14% cost of capital, and low on anything that requires sizing robotaxi revenue, because no revenue line, fare or cost per mile is disclosed. The 2026-10-25 consensus is Hold across 48 firms with a $408.61 average target and a published range from $128.11 to $600, so the disagreement is about the distribution, not the mean. [S141, S144, S4]

What is Tesla's revenue per robotaxi per week in Austin, and what share of those rides runs without a safety driver?

Without that number the autonomy value cannot be tested against a cost per mile, and every scenario above the bear case rests on a registry count of authorised vehicles rather than on unit economics. A disclosed figure that supports the revenue per mile the price implies would move the base case toward the bull case; a quarter of silence after three years of promises would move it toward the bear case. Waymo's own published rides per vehicle per week set the utilisation bar Tesla's Austin fleet has to beat.

1. **The price is the whole debate:** $360.30 of the $403.30 — 89% — is autonomy and robotics valued at 11.3 times Waymo's $126B, and the core business is worth $43.00 on vehicles at 1.0x sales, energy at 3.5x, services at 1.0x and net cash at book [S15, S120].
2. **Cash is thinner than it looks:** 61% less free cash flow in nine months, a $7,332M payables stretch and a 5.5% ROIC against an 11-14% cost of capital, with $20B+ of capex still to come [S4].
3. **One event can change the call:** a premium exchange ratio into SpaceX would pay $443-464 without any robotaxi revenue, but the vote needs 50% of all shares, no terms are agreed, and a failed vote returns the stock below $300 [S135, S5].

The follow-up diligence is dated and specific: a robotaxi revenue line, a fleet count and a fare in the next results release; a California driverless deployment permit from the DMV and CPUC filings, where the current service runs on a limousine authority; the exchange ratio, advisers and treatment of unvested awards in the special committees' 8-K; capital expenditure guidance, the Terafab contribution and any payables reversal in the annual 10-K; and the per-tranche thresholds of the CEO award in the proxy for the 2026-12-03 annual meeting. The rating is a statement about the price of an option, not about the quality of the engineering: the vehicle, cell and storage businesses are real, and they are worth about a tenth of what the market pays.

## 公司概览 Company Overview

Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer [S3].

EX-21 states no ownership percentages, so the ownership column above is inferred from listing rather than disclosed. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, with 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage, software (1.74 million FSD subscriptions) and paying Cybercab rides in Austin since 2026-09-03.

| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | 74.9% | 74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float is capped by those stakes, and a margin call on the pledged block would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's dual-class family control or Alphabet's founder shares.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel, a director, runs Redwood Materials, a Tesla supplier. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors carrying outside ties — Ehrenpreis and Kimbal Musk to SpaceX, Straubel to Redwood Materials, a Tesla supplier — two of those to SpaceX itself; the proxy's retail auto-voting programme adds standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: the Special Committee used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, so cash returned to holders is zero while insiders realise value through equity sales. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for four things: a contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; new debt against a thin free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, no change-of-control acceleration without operating milestones, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure, medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value.

## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel

Tesla's execution machine still ships, but the bench beneath Elon Musk has thinned to three named executive officers and at least 17 senior departures since April 2024, so a four-front roadmap in vehicles, energy, autonomy and robots rests on one man and a handful of engineers paid to stay rather than on a management team that could be handed the plan. The disclosed leadership is Musk (CEO and Technoking, age 55), Vaibhav Taneja (CFO since August 2023) and Xiaotong (Tom) Zhu (SVP APAC and Global Vehicle Manufacturing since June 2025), with no chief operating officer, president or segment chief between them and a nine-person board. Salaries are $400,000 for Taneja and $364,338 for Zhu, and Musk has taken none since 2019, so retention runs through equity, not cash [S5].

On execution the record is binary rather than average. Tesla produced its 10 millionth vehicle in Q3 2026, began volume production of the Semi, started Megafactory Texas and put Optimus onto a high-volume line at Fremont; Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year, with 13.7 GWh of storage deployed and 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions [S6]. The 4680 cell gives the counter-rhythm: dry-electrode production for both anode and cathode arrived only with the Q4 2025 update, five years after the Battery Day target, and management still called battery availability the limiting factor for vehicle volumes in Q3 2026. Tesla solves hard manufacturing problems and solves them late, so a roadmap that now includes Cybercab, Optimus, a lithium refinery, an AI6 chip programme and Megafactory Texas should be discounted on that lag rather than on the best-case line.

Turnover is the counter-evidence, and it clusters where the growth story sits. At least 17 senior leaders left between April 2024 and 2026-10-15: the Cybercab programme lost its program manager (Victor Nechita, February 2026), its new-product-introduction head (Michael So, April 2026), two assembly leaders and the director who built robotaxi software (Thomas Dmytryk, March 2026); energy lost vice president Mike Snyder on 2026-10-15, succeeded by AJ Booth; finance lost Sendil Palani after 17 years in March 2026; and sales lost two North American chiefs in a year, including Raj Jegannathan in February 2026 [S93]. Internal promotion is real — Joe Ward went from European operations to global sales chief in February 2026 — but the pattern is that programme leaders are replaced by narrower specialists while the number of programmes grows.

The autonomy bench rests on one person. Ashok Elluswamy joined in 2014 as the first Autopilot engineer, led the removal of radar, built the end-to-end FSD architecture and now runs FSD, Robotaxi software and Optimus AI, plus a joint project with xAI; he holds none of the disclosed executive-officer titles, so he appears in neither the proxy ownership table nor the summary compensation table [S94]. Losing him would hit three programmes at once, and the retention tools available are the same volatile equity that has already seen software and AI staff leave for OpenAI and rivals. Depth is real in manufacturing — the Semi and Megafactory ramps show an operations bench that can still deliver — but the layer where autonomy and energy execution actually happens has lost the people who built it.

Founder-market fit is strongest where the problem is physics and manufacturing, weakest where it is regulated operations. Musk's career — Zip2 and PayPal sold to Compaq and eBay, then SpaceX and Tesla built from near-zero — is a serial-building record, and the full vesting of his first performance award is the market's own evidence that he hits market-capitalisation and operating targets. The gaps are structural: a chief operating officer who could own delivery across four programmes, a robotics manufacturing executive with volume experience, a regulatory leader able to win driverless approvals in the European Union and China, and an enterprise energy sales organisation that converts a record order book into contracted revenue. None of those roles appears in the proxy, so each is either unfilled or sits below the executive-officer line, and both readings raise execution risk at the scale the valuation implies.

The judgement is a conditional, not a rejection. Tesla's engineering culture has repeatedly converted improbable hardware into shipping product, and the board has paid to keep the one person who drives that conversion. What it has not built is an organisation that can lose him, or lose the programme leaders beneath him, without slowing. An investor holding through the robotaxi and Optimus ramp should size for announcement risk and ask three questions: who owns delivery of each programme if Musk or Elluswamy is unavailable, what retention has been granted below the executive-officer line, and whether the Cybercab departures reflected a programme reset the company has not disclosed. Confidence is high on team composition and the departure record, medium on what that turnover implies for 2027 timelines, because Tesla does not disclose programme-level staffing.

**Strongest proof the team can execute** is the compounding of hard manufacturing inside one quarter: 10.2 million cumulative vehicles, a Semi line running, Megafactory Texas in production, Optimus on a high-volume line and paying Cybercab rides, with 1.74 million FSD subscriptions and 13.7 GWh of storage alongside them [S6].

**Strongest doubt** is that the same quarter produced a 2% delivery decline while the Cybercab programme lost four leaders and energy lost its vice president two weeks before this report, so the programmes that must justify the valuation are the ones losing the people who built them, and the CEO who would absorb their decisions also runs SpaceX [S93].

## 技术与产品 Technology & Product

Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits, judged against two comparison sets: Waymo in autonomy and BYD in manufacturing cost. Compared with Waymo, Tesla has 2.0 million cumulative autonomous miles against 500,000 paid rides a week on 4,000 vehicles; compared with BYD, its 486,532 quarterly deliveries trail BYD's 762,478 electric cars. Its paid driverless permit exists in one state. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform [S6, S59, S76, S107].

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only: eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking, trained on video from 10.2 million delivered vehicles and run on in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar or radar. Two problems stay unsolved. Cameras blinded by rain, fog or low sun are the subject of NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes in 2.88 million vehicles, testing whether the system detects the degradation. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to Q2 2027. Tesla's October 2026 report claims 6,006,200 miles per major collision, a company-computed, non-fault-based figure the regulator has not verified [S58, S80].

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Tesla publishes no fleet count of its own. Tesla's Texas fleet stood at 1,051 authorised vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y, Texas DMV records); NHTSA's DP26010 puts the population it is reviewing at 1,000, its estimate and an exposure ceiling rather than an active count; paid Cybercab service has run in Austin since 2026-09-03. Registrations record authorisations, not vehicles in service, and Tesla discloses no fares, trips per vehicle, utilisation or insurance cost per mile. Permits remain the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC for testing with a driver only (2026-10-22) [S73, S118, S150, S151, S152].

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost 50% lower at full scale, 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026 at a 33.1% gross margin, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. The weak point is the order book, not the product: the 2026-10-21 update claims a record order rate and backlog, but Tesla discloses neither GWh nor dollars of contracted backlog, so the claim is unverified. A contracted-backlog figure or 2027 deployments above the 36.0 GWh nine-month run at stable revenue per GWh would confirm it; a third quarter of falling revenue per GWh would contradict it. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among integrators behind Sungrow, and revenue fell 16% to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S6, S72].

**The Optimus output target is an unverified company claim, and the humanoid benchmark sits elsewhere.**

On the Q3 2026 call of 2026-10-21 Tesla set a target of 20,000 Optimus units a week by end-2027 and began early production, but it discloses no unit count, external customer, task list or revenue. A named customer, supplier orders at that volume or an Optimus revenue line would confirm it; another year of demonstration video and no billed unit would contradict it. Figure AI, valued at $39bn in September 2025, completed an 11-month Figure 02 deployment at BMW's Spartanburg plant contributing to more than 30,000 X3 vehicles, the external validation Optimus has not matched [S57, S149].

### What would change the judgement

The strongest counter-case is that FSD is already monetised: attach, subscriptions and deferred revenue rose in Q3 2026. Against it, repeated NHTSA recalls on the 2026 Model Y show launch quality slipping, and the attach rate is North American only while China sales fell with FSD approval pending. Optimus is the thinner half of the autonomy branch: a production line and no external customer.

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor, and what fare, trips per vehicle and insurance cost per mile sit behind that revenue? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not proven the one the share price pays for.

## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis

Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. No plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, with incentives of $6,594 per vehicle. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units, a 0.95 million unit annual run-rate at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, while hybrids took 36.6%. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6%. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced by the 2026 energy-price shock. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved Tesla's way for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

### Market size: $950 billion of cars, $83 billion of storage

The 2026 market size is $950 billion for electric cars and $82.7 billion for grid storage, measured at Tesla's realised prices as a proxy because no agency publishes revenue; global electric-car units rise from an implied 16.7 million in 2024 to 23.0 million in 2026, a 17.4% compound annual growth rate, and the battery-electric slice of the three regions where Tesla sells is not published, so the table bounds obtainable revenue rather than measuring the serviceable market. Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply: 353.4 GWh of deployments are expected in 2026, up 28% on 275.3 GWh in 2025, and Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in nine months, 14% of the market, against 50 GWh of Texas capacity. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer behind an interconnection queue, so demand is sticky but price-sensitive: energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 to $2,881 million on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Ride-hailing cannot yet be sized from disclosure: Waymo operates 4,000 vehicles (TechCrunch's 2026-09-24 fleet estimate) and reports 500,000 paid rides a week, 26 million a year; even at $100 a ride that is $2.6 billion, 0.3% of the electric-car TAM, while Tesla discloses no fare, booking or paid-ride figure. Tesla's Texas fleet stood at 1,051 authorised vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y; TxDMV registry via TeslaNorth and Drive Tesla Canada), with no in-service count disclosed; NHTSA's DP26010 puts the population it is reviewing at 1,000, its estimate and an exposure ceiling rather than an active count; paid Cybercab service has run in Austin since 2026-09-03 [S100, S108, S4, S59, S150, S154, S152, S153].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement: if US battery-electric share holds for four quarters, the credit will have been worth two-fifths of US demand, and a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the robotaxi market forward. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides or bookings. Three open diligence questions remain: what did US battery-electric share print in September-October 2026? What share of Giga Shanghai output was exported in Q3 2026? What was Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh excluding tariff refunds?

**US battery-electric demand stepped down to a new level after the credit expired and has not recovered a year later**

US BEV share of light-duty sales was 6% in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8%; the luxury segment fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. Cox Automotive recorded a $54,754 average transaction price with incentives of $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit, yet August volume still fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units [S98, S103].

## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape

Tesla is gaining share in the markets that are shrinking and holding share in the one that is growing, so its vehicle advantage is compressing into a cost-and-brand moat rather than a technology lead, while in storage it is a scale follower to CATL and BYD and in paid autonomy it reports no ride volume against Waymo's 500,000 a week. Three numbers show it: a 51.7% share of US EV sales in August 2026, European registrations up 51% to 153,978 in 9M 2026, and Chinese retail down 11.9% to 381,088 in a market down 12.5% [S103, S104, S102].

### In the United States, Tesla wins by attrition

Tesla sold 40,816 EVs in August 2026 for 51.7% of US EV sales, up 3.4 points from July, in a market that fell 46.9% to 78,895 units. Behind it the gains were small (Toyota 4,964 units, +34.9% month on month; Chevrolet +30.3%; Cadillac +13.1%), and weaker EV programmes retreated after the credit expired, letting the widest-line, lowest-cost survivor take share without cutting price. Rivian could change the arithmetic: its mid-size SUV has sold since Q2 2026 from a Normal, Illinois plant with 215,000 units of annual capacity [S103, S96].

### Europe is a battery-electric contest; China is a price contest

In an 11-country European panel Tesla registered 45,523 cars in September 2026 against BYD's 39,583, and on battery-electric only led 30,317 to 7,498, while Chinese brands as a group took 14.9% of new cars against 8.0% a year earlier. BYD's route into Europe is powertrain breadth and price, not a better battery car, which makes it the most dangerous competitor over five years: it builds volume below Model Y and can move up. In China the contest is worse: Model Y sold more than 180,000 units from February to July 2026 at RMB 263,500-313,500 while Geely's Xingyuan sold nearly 197,500 at just under RMB 100,000 (~$14,820), and Tesla's domestic retail fell 11.9% while Shanghai wholesale held only on a 58.3% September export rise. Two closer threats sit in Model Y's band: Xpeng delivered 41,256 in September 2026 (−0.78% year on year) and launched the G9L on 2026-09-17 from RMB 231,800 (~$34,420), while Huawei's HIMA delivered 367,229 in January-September 2026, within 4% of Tesla's 381,088 China retail, with the updated AITO M8 from RMB 389,800 (~$57,880) [S104, S101, S102, S155, S156, S157].

### Pricing power is real in the premium band and absent below it

Q3 2026 automotive cost of revenue of $16,754 million over 486,532 deliveries is $34,436 per vehicle, against automotive revenue of $20,560 million, or $42,258 per unit: an 18.5% automotive gross margin, up from 17.0%. The margin is healthy at a premium price point and rests on mix, credits and software, not price: regulatory credits fell to $113 million from $417 million, FSD (Supervised) subscriptions reached 1.74 million, services and other revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million, and energy gross margin reached 33.1%. The $34,436 is 2.3 times the retail price of China's volume bestseller, the Geely Xingyuan at just under RMB 100,000 (~$14,820), the gap a $25,000-35,000 price war would expose [S4, S6, S101].

### Storage and autonomy are where the advantage is thinnest

In grid storage pricing power sits with the cell makers: CATL shipped 125.0 GWh of energy-storage batteries in H1 2026, up 81%, for 27.1% of the global ESS cell market, while Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in nine months and energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 to $2,881 million on lower Megapack prices and tariff refunds. Tesla differentiates on integration and delivery speed, not cell cost. In autonomy the gap is disclosed scale: Waymo operates 4,000 vehicles (TechCrunch's 2026-09-24 estimate) and reports 500,000 paid rides a week, while Baidu's Apollo Go runs in more than 10 Chinese cities and Tesla publishes no paid-ride count. Tesla's Texas fleet stood at 1,051 authorised vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y; TxDMV registry via TeslaNorth and Drive Tesla Canada), with no in-service count disclosed; NHTSA's DP26010 puts the population it is reviewing at 1,000, its estimate and an exposure ceiling rather than an active count; paid Cybercab service has run in Austin since 2026-09-03 [S81, S4, S59, S150, S154, S152, S153].

| Grid battery storage | Tesla challenges | CATL: 27.1% of ESS cells | Tesla: 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 | Fluence and Sungrow | Chinese LFP integrators | S81, S4 |
| Robotaxi | Tesla emerges | Waymo: 4,000 vehicles, 500,000 paid rides a week | Baidu Apollo Go: more than 10 cities | Zoox and Pony.ai | Tesla Cybercab | S59, S6 |

The counter-case is conversion rather than loss: US and European share gains came while rivals retreated, automotive gross margin rose year on year, and the Chinese price war ended with more than a dozen automakers raising prices. Partly right, but the gains sit in shrinking pools and the margin gain is mix-driven, not price-driven. Confidence is high on US and European share data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions differ, low on autonomy because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Two questions follow: Tesla's US EV share in Q4 2026 as Toyota's bZ and Chevrolet's Bolt ramp, and how much of BYD's European volume is plug-in hybrid under the 2027 CO2 review?

**Tesla's competitive position is strongest where the market is shrinking and weakest where it is growing**

Tesla held 51.7% of US EV sales in August 2026 in a market down 46.9% year on year, registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country European panel in 9M 2026 (+51%), and sold 381,088 cars in China (-11.9%), where Huawei's HIMA delivered 367,229 and Xpeng 284,367 in the same nine months. Its $34,436 cost per vehicle is 2.3 times Geely's sub-RMB 100,000 retail price, CATL holds 27.1% of ESS cells, and Tesla reports no paid-ride figure against Waymo's 500,000 a week; the Texas count is authorisation, not service [S103, S104, S102, S4, S81, S59, S150, S155, S156].

## 商业模式 Business Model

Tesla still sells cars for a living, but in 2026 its incremental profit comes from energy storage and services while regulatory credits fade, and the car business alone does not cover its cost base. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%). Cash arrives on delivery, on storage milestones and customer prepayments ($3.30 billion of deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came with the 2026 removal of the compliance obligation, not the lapse of the consumer credit: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while automotive cost of revenue per delivery (total automotive cost of revenue divided by deliveries) fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific mix from the low-cost Shanghai plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 includes corporate cost and the first vehicle's gross profit covers it 1.8 times. A three-year LTV of $8,455 — three years of services gross profit at $288 a vehicle on 10.2 million deliveries — gives LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million on 13.7 GWh deployed, up from 12.5 GWh, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026 and Megafactory Texas began production with planned capacity of 50 GWh. On the backlog, management said on the 2026-10-21 earnings call that Tesla is "almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027", and the same day's release cites a "highest-ever order rate and backlog" — company claims only, unverified, with no volume, contract value or price disclosed, so the energy annuity has to be sized on reported deployments, not on the backlog. Fluence earned 13.1%; Tesla's edge is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million — a company operating KPI defined for the 2025 CEO Performance Award, not an audited or GAAP-reported metric — while deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue [S6, S63, S67, S158].

The newest change in money flows is who owns the asset: a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile rather than per delivery. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested; until then the investable model remains cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is the cost base: $4,776 million of operating expenses needs $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin; Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing the energy and services annuity on reported deployments and contracted revenue, not on the undisclosed 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the cost base alone. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic, medium on how much of the cost relief is structural. Four diligence questions remain: what is the North American automotive margin excluding credits? What is the energy margin excluding tariff refunds, and what volumes and prices underpin the claimed 2027 Megapack sell-out? Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue and robotaxi recognition? When do R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue? [S4, S6]

**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].

## 财务分析 Financial Analysis

Tesla's earnings do not justify its premium, and the cash behind them is thinning. At $403.30 on 2026-10-29 the equity is worth $1,594.1 billion on 3,952.6 million shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, or $1,558.0 billion of enterprise value after $36.2 billion of net cash: on the enterprise value, 15.0 times trailing revenue of $103,570 million, 104 times adjusted EBITDA of $14,995 million and 450 times operating income; on the market capitalisation, 443.2 times trailing diluted EPS of $0.91 (net income $3,218 million on 3,541 million diluted shares) and 483 times trailing free cash flow of $3,303 million [S1, S2, S3, S4, S6, S15]. Revenue went from $81,462 million in FY2022 to $96,773 million, $97,690 million and $94,827 million, while operating income fell from $13,656 million to $8,891 million, $7,076 million and $4,355 million, and the operating margin from 16.8% to 2.6% in nine months of 2026. Gross margin held between 17.9% and 19.0% from FY2023, so the compression is operating expense: R&D rose from $3,969 million in FY2023 to $6,411 million in FY2025 and $7,078 million in nine months of 2026. FY2023's $14,997 million net income included a $5,001 million income tax benefit, so the fall to $3,794 million in FY2025 understates the decline in pre-tax earnings.

Revenue of $28,046 million was flat in Q3 2026, gross profit rose 8.7% to $5,494 million, and operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39%, leaving operating income of $718 million, down 56%, and net income of $787 million, down 43%, or $0.22 diluted against $0.39. Non-GAAP net income was $1,697 million, or $0.48 against $0.50; the $910 million gap is chiefly $1,165 million of stock-based compensation, partly offset by the excluded $288 million Bitcoin gain and $142 million SpaceX write-down. Pretax income exceeded operating income by $238 million, 30% of net income, and the effective tax rate fell to 16% from 29% partly on a state deferred-tax release. Automotive cost of revenue per vehicle delivered was $34,436, down 2.7% on 486,532 deliveries [S4, S6].

Cash generation now depends on working capital: supplier balances and customer prepayments are growing faster than earnings. Operating cash flow rose 36% to $14,897 million while net income fell 19.5% to $2,378 million; payables and accrued liabilities contributed $7,332 million against $2,979 million a year earlier, accounts payable rose to $17,239 million from $13,371 million at 2025-12-31, and days payables outstanding went from 62.8 to 75.3. Deferred revenue added $1,746 million, mostly storage prepayments that rose to $3.30 billion. Capital expenditure of $13,014 million consumed 87% of operating cash flow, and quarterly free cash flow was $1,444 million, negative $1,092 million and $1,531 million, against $3,990 million in Q3 2025. Depreciation of $4,290 million rose 17% and will climb faster than revenue as more than $20 billion of 2026 spending is commissioned [S3, S4, S6].

The balance sheet is not the constraint; the return on the capital being deployed is. At 2026-09-30 Tesla held $45,447 million of cash and short-term investments against $9,267 million of debt, or $36,180 million of net cash, and signed $30 billion of credit commitments in September 2026. Goodwill is 0.2% of assets; the pressure is in inventory of $14,092 million, up 13.7% since 2025-12-31 while deliveries fell 2%, and a warranty reserve of $10,138 million, up 26%. Invested capital of $53,109 million earned 5.5% after tax on a trailing basis (TTM net operating profit after tax over average invested capital for the four quarters to 2026-09-30), against 28.3% in FY2023; the roughly 3% return on 2026 invested capital that includes the full capital programme is a forward-looking figure on a larger asset base, not a competing measurement of the same period [S4].

Against a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.5 to 2.0, our estimate of the cost of capital is 11% to 14%, so the company destroys economic value at current margins. Capital allocation offers no offset: no dividend or buyback, capex guided above $20 billion for 2026, and $1.95 billion of stock paid for an AI hardware company in Q2 2026. Equity compensation is the other claim on shareholders: $3,346 million in nine months is 4.3% of revenue; the 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7 million shares, 10.7% of the 3,952.6 million outstanding, with $9.74 billion of unrecognised expense on the one milestone judged probable (20 million vehicles, recognised over 8.9 years) and $105.82-120.37 billion on the remaining tranches. The economic reading is that Tesla is converting a vehicle and cell cost advantage into a capital-intensive compute and robotics business before that business has customers, so the shares trade on optionality rather than earnings [S4, S15, S24].

Tesla trades at 443.2 times trailing diluted EPS of $0.91, 24 times the peer median of 18.5 times earnings, and at 15.0 times sales, 6.3 times the median 2.4 times sales; market capitalisation over the same $3,218 million of net income is 495 times. Adjusted EBITDA is struck before stock-based compensation, so 104 times is understated as a cash multiple. Each 100 basis points of automotive gross margin excluding credits is worth $756 million, or $0.19 a share, on $75,561 million of nine-month automotive revenue, so a two-point margin miss plus a $4 billion capex overshoot would take 2027 free cash flow to roughly negative $2 billion, while energy growth of 40% at a 30% margin and a 20% automotive margin would lift it to about $8 billion. The contrast shows the strategic problem: the market is paying for autonomy and robotics because the vehicle and storage businesses cannot support the multiple on these returns, so position size should be set by tolerance for a de-rating from 104 times EBITDA, not by near-term cash generation. Confidence is high on the statements and the cash bridge, medium on the cost of capital and low on any estimate that requires autonomous revenue to be sized. Three diligence questions remain: how much of the payables increase reverses in Q4 2026? What is the split of the 2026 capital budget between maintenance and AI compute? Does the board intend to offset dilution from the performance award? [S15, S17, S19, S21, S111, S113, S121]

**Operating cash flow is financed by suppliers, not by earnings**
Payables and accrued liabilities supplied most of the increase in nine-month operating cash flow while net income fell, and payment days sit at a multi-year high. With equity compensation at a multi-year high share of revenue and a one-off state tax release in the tax line, both the cash and the profit are weaker than reported, and when supplier terms normalise operating cash flow converges on earnings on low single-digit margins.

## 融资历程与估值 Funding History & Valuation

At $403.30 (NasdaqGS, 2026-10-29 20:00 UTC) Tesla's equity is worth $1,594.1B and its enterprise value $1,558.0B. On a sum of the parts, 89% of that price — $1,424B, or $360.30 a share — buys autonomy and robotics, while the automotive, energy and services businesses plus $36.2B of net cash are worth $43.00 a share at peer multiples. That residual is 11.3 times the $126B at which Waymo raised $16B in February 2026, and Waymo is the only operator running a scaled driverless service. My probability-weighted value is $111 a share, 72.5% below the close; the disagreement is not about cars, since my $43.00 for the core sits within $5 of Morgan Stanley's $47, but about whether 2.0M cumulative unsupervised miles, a robotaxi service confined to one city and zero disclosed Optimus revenue can carry $1.4 trillion. [S15, S120, S6]

### Sum of the parts: $43.00 of business, and a bear case of $19

Trailing-twelve-month segment data from the Q3 2026 update: automotive revenue $75.0B at a 19.1% gross margin, energy $12.3B at 29.7%, services $16.3B at 12.4%, sharing $16.5B of operating expense. At 1.0x sales for vehicles and services — 2.5x GM's implied 0.39x, warranted by double GM's gross margin — 3.5x for energy (above Fluence's 0.5x) and net cash at book, the core is $170B, or $43.00 a share on the 3,952.6M shares behind the $1,594.1B capitalisation. The 4.00B fully diluted count that adds 710M unvested award shares (18%) gives $42.50 as a dilution sensitivity, and on 3,240M basic shares today's equity is $1,307B, not $1,594B. The base case's $259B of autonomy is an explicit tree — 35% × $40B regional, 40% × $126B at Waymo's licensing value, 20% × $600B multi-metro, 5% × $1,500B global dominance — $65.5 a share. The bear case is the same arithmetic with each input cut: autonomy, FSD and Optimus at zero; vehicles at 0.39x automotive revenue, a 10% discount to GM's 0.43x on $72.3B of market capitalisation over $169.8B of revenue, giving $29.3B on $75.0B; energy at 1.5x its $12.3B, or $18.4B, less than half the base multiple; and net cash cut to $28B from $36.2B after a year of capital spending and recall costs. That sum is $75.6B, $18.91 a share. Adding $259B of autonomy to the $170B core gives $429B, $107 on the diluted count ($108.50 on shares outstanding); the core with $600B gives $847B, $212. Weighting 25/50/25 on $212/$107/$19 gives $111, 72.5% below the price. Scenario per-share values divide by the 4.00B fully diluted count (3,952.6M outstanding plus 710M unvested award shares), a 1.2% dilution sensitivity; the headline uses shares outstanding. ### The reverse DCF needs sixteen million robotaxis

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, on $2.0B of 2027 free cash flow growing 45% a year, today's enterprise value requires $141B of 2031 free cash flow (9% WACC: $118B; 11%: $164B). At a 15% margin that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing. At a 25% robotaxi margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue: at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, 15.7M robotaxis — 7.8M if cars and energy supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet six years of full capacity could not build at a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges. [S4, S6]

### What the street pays for, and what would prove it right

The consensus twelve-month target is $408.61 from 48 analysts on 2026-10-25, 1.3% above the close, range $128.11-$600 — a 4.7x spread that measures uncertainty, not value. Short interest is 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float, 2.2 days to cover: no crowded short, no positioning signal. Management publishes no numeric guidance, promising only "maximum capacity utilization". Dated catalysts are the 2026-12-03 annual meeting, Q4 2026 results in late January 2027, Austin Fab tool commissioning in 2027 and the special-committee process opened on 2026-10-20 — the one event that could re-rate the shares without an operating delivery. [S141, S144, S6, S114]

The counter-evidence is real. Tesla has held a triple-digit multiple for two years without mean reversion; the 2025 CEO award ties 423.7M shares to market-cap milestones to $8.5T, aligning management with the narrative rather than with per-share cash flow; and a merger into SpaceX at $2.1T would give Tesla holders 43% of a $3.7T company with Starlink cash flows, against which a standalone sum of the parts is the wrong instrument. But stock compensation runs at 4.2% of revenue and every award tranche is paid in shares. The margin of safety at $403.30 is negative and turns positive only below $111; between those levels the buyer is purchasing an option and should size it as one. [S132]

Confidence is high on the core-business value and low on the autonomy tree. What would settle it: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile; the Austin fleet count and utilisation; the thresholds of each award tranche; 2026 capital expenditure guidance; and the exchange ratio the special committees would accept.

## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy

Tesla's strategy has become a capital-allocation bet rather than an operating one: more than $20bn of 2026 capex and $30bn of new credit facilities are committed to autonomy, robots and semiconductors while nine-month 2026 operating income of $2.06bn implies a return on invested capital near 3%, below any plausible cost of capital. The strategy earns its keep only if unsupervised robotaxi revenue arrives before 2028, and the 12-month test is customer-owned unsupervised driving in mid-2027, not another reveal [S4, S78].

### The plan and the return do not yet match

Tesla guided in the Q3 2026 filing to capital expenditure above $20bn for 2026, after spending $13.01bn in the first nine months against $6.13bn a year earlier, and in September 2026 signed three credit agreements for aggregate commitments of $30bn. Cash and short-term investments were $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 against $9.5bn of debt, so the plan is funded; it is no longer self-funding. Nine-month operating income of $2.06bn on $89.29bn of equity, annualised after tax over roughly $71bn of invested capital, gives a return near 3% — depressed by ramp assets, but low enough that every further billion of capex lowers the return until the new assets sell something [S6]. Research and development rose 69% year over year to $2.76bn in Q3 2026, most of it for autonomy and robotics.

### Pricing and mix are carrying the capex

The read is that Tesla is funding autonomy from a mature car business, a fading credit stream and a fast-growing but deflating storage business; none of the three is a rising price. The Semi is a logical adjacency because it shares cells, motors and Megachargers with the core; Optimus is not an adjacency yet, because it has a production line and no customer.

The partner map shows the strategic risk: Tesla's autonomy roadmap runs through a single foundry for AI6, its vehicles still depend on CATL, Panasonic and LG for cells, and its largest related-party exposure is to companies its chief executive also controls.

### Geography: China becomes an export base

Tesla's China sales fell 16% year over year in Q3 2026 to 142,133 units while Giga Shanghai exports reached a record 132,978; retail sales for 2026 to date are down 12% as exports doubled, and Beijing cuts the EV export tax rebate in April 2027. Shanghai, with more than 950,000 units of capacity, is now a cost and export base rather than a growth market, exposed to tariffs in the markets it ships to. Berlin set a production record and the US business carries the FSD attach rate, which is why the company's own numbers look better in North America than in the two regions that decide its cost base [S77, S76, S102].

### Energy is where the strategy is working

The energy plan is coherent and funded: 50 GWh of Megafactory Texas capacity started in Q3 2026 alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai, with 7 GWh of Nevada LFP cell capacity in early ramp and the first Megapacks built from Tesla-made cells. The 2026-10-21 update claims a record order rate and backlog, but Tesla discloses neither GWh nor dollars of contracted backlog, so the claim is unverified: a contracted-backlog figure or 2027 deployments above the 36.0 GWh nine-month run at stable revenue per GWh would confirm it, and a third quarter of falling revenue per GWh would contradict it. A 33.1% segment gross margin and data-centre demand give the capital a return that autonomy does not yet. The tension is that revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose, so the plan is adding capacity into falling prices [S6, S72].

### The capital allocation question

In January 2026 Tesla invested $2bn in xAI; the stake became SpaceX Class A shares when SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026, and the Q1 2026 cash flow statement records a $2.002bn purchase of SpaceX equity. Three of nine directors carry outside ties — two to SpaceX (Ehrenpreis and Kimbal Musk), one to Straubel at Redwood Materials, a Tesla supplier — and the committee uses two. The 2026 proxy is set for a 2026-12-03 meeting, and the 2025 CEO award pays out on a deal price without operational milestones — only one of twelve operational milestones is rated probable, leaving $105.8-120.4bn of unrecognised stock compensation. A shareholder is no longer buying only a car and storage company; a merger scenario makes the position a bet on Musk's wider portfolio, which argues for a smaller size [S78].

### What must be true in 12 months

Three signposts decide whether the strategy is earning its cost of capital. First, unsupervised driving in customer-owned cars in at least one US state by 2027-06-30, with robotaxi revenue disclosed separately — without it, the capex is a subsidy to a pilot. Second, energy gross margin holding above 25% once tariff refunds lapse and 50 GWh of Texas capacity ramps, which tests whether Megapack has pricing power or is a commodity; the unverified backlog claim needs a contracted figure or 2027 deployments above 36.0 GWh to become evidence. Third, capital discipline: 2027 capex at or below $25bn with positive free cash flow, rather than a further draw on the $30bn facilities. The humanoid plan needs its first named customer or billed unit before a 20,000-a-week target means anything. The counter-case is strong: FSD attach above 75% in North America, 1.74 million subscriptions, a record energy backlog and $45.45bn of cash mean the plan can be funded through a slip, and Q3 2026 free cash flow of $1.53bn shows the core still generates cash [S6, S57].

Diligence questions: what is the 2027 capex number and how much of it is contractually committed? What revenue did robotaxi and FSD each earn in Q3 2026? Will the December 2026 meeting put a SpaceX transaction to a shareholder vote, and on what terms? My confidence is high that the strategy is funded and well-resourced for energy, medium that autonomy revenue arrives before 2028, and low that a humanoid robot contributes to profit before 2029.

## 风险评估 Risk Assessment

At $403.30 on 2026-10-29 Tesla is a $1,594.1B equity split $43.00 a share, $170B, for the vehicle, energy, services and net-cash business and $360.30 a share, $1,424B, for autonomy and robotics; on 25/50/25 of $212/$107/$19 the probability-weighted value is $111, so the share is a reduce and new money is an option purchase. A market 50% smaller leaves a $105B core, $26 a share, at 94% autonomy; CAC doubled adds $8.1B; revenue 30% lower removes $6.0B; a 5.0x multiple on free cash flow 30% lower is $130; financing six months late is covered by the September facilities [S6, S15, S120, S4, S115]. None reverses the conclusion; a premium exchange ratio does, the risk the recommendation must price. The three premises carrying the $1,424B are deteriorating at once: NHTSA's Cybercab self-certification inquiry closes for comment on 2026-10-30, the special committees formed on 2026-10-20 have no terms, and nine-month free cash flow of $1,883M contains $7,332M from stretching payables to 75.3 days.

### The core is not harsh at 1.0x sales; it is generous

The sum of the parts pays $91B for vehicles and services at 1.0x sales, $43B for energy at 3.5x and $36B of net cash at book. At GM's implied 0.39x, vehicles and services are worth $29B and the core is $87B, $21.75 a share, with autonomy at 95% of the price; a control buyer tops out at $200-250B, $50-62.50, where autonomy still holds 84%. Energy's 3.5x has support — a 29.7% gross margin against Fluence's 13.1% — but doubling revenue to $25B on 5.0x adds $82B, $20 a share, and FSD's 1.74M subscribers at $1,200 a year add $42B, $10.5, leaving the best honest core near $70, autonomy at 83%. The $1,424B premium is 11.3 times Waymo's $126B mark, for 1,051 Texas-authorised vehicles against Waymo's 4,000. [S6, S131, S120, S15, S151]

### The scenario tree is generous at the base and shallow in the bear

The base case's $259B of autonomy is an explicit tree — 35% x $40B regional, 40% x $126B at Waymo parity, 20% x $600B at scale, 5% x $1,500B at dominance — and $259B is 2.1x Waymo's $126B for a fleet with nine reported crashes in August 2026 and no disclosed revenue per mile. Tesla's Texas fleet stood at 1,051 authorised vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y, Texas DMV records); NHTSA's DP26010 puts the population under review at 1,000, an estimate and exposure ceiling, not an active count; paid Cybercab service has run in Austin since 2026-09-03. Waymo operates 4,000 vehicles (TechCrunch's 2026-09-24 fleet estimate) and reports 500,000 paid rides a week. On the regional branch alone the base is $53, with the tree's $84 weighted value 79% below the close, and the 40% probabilities for 2027 unsupervised FSD and a merger sit above the record: EA26002 covers 2.88M vehicles and DP26010 opened on 2026-10-09. An NHTSA rejection has a 35% probability and a $45-90 a share impact. The $35 bear was too shallow: at $19 — autonomy at zero, vehicles at 0.39x, energy at 1.5x, net cash $29B after a Terafab call — the drawdown is 95% and the weighted value falls only from $115 to $111. Above $437 the path is a 10-15% ratio premium, $443-464. [S120, S137, S6, S5, S150, S151, S152, S153, S59]

### Cash carries a two-year slip, not a slip plus a revenue fall

Net cash of $36.18B and $30B of facilities signed in September 2026 carry a two-year autonomy slip at zero free cash flow without issuing a share. The combination does not survive a revenue fall: at a 19% gross margin, 30% lower revenue removes $6.0B of gross profit against $19.1B of annual operating expense, so with $20-25B of capex the annual burn is $20-27B and cash plus facilities run out before 2029. Reported cash flow already borrows from suppliers: payables and accruals added $7,332M and days payable rose from 62.8 to 75.3, worth $2.9B, so normalised free cash flow is minus $1.0B. Terafab adds a commitment Tesla does not control: a $16.8B first phase with SpaceX, Tesla's share undisclosed, outside the ">$20B" 2026 capital budget and called a "general framework" with no binding commitment in SpaceX's IPO filing — capping near-term cash risk and weakening the strategic-asset defence. Tesla is Baa3, SpaceX Baa1; the facilities' pricing is undisclosed. [S4, S134, S138, S147]

### The merger is an option, not a floor

On 2026-10-20 Musk said both boards had formed special committees, no terms agreed and none assured; the Tesla vote needs 50% of all shares, not of those cast, so abstentions count against, and the 2026-10-19 proxy sets the 2026-12-03 annual meeting with no merger proposal. At market the deal is value-neutral: $1,594.1B plus SpaceX's $2.01T is $3.60T, and Tesla holders taking 43-44% own today's price; any premium must be conceded by SpaceX. Either way Tesla holders get 43% of the economics; 84% of votes sit with one holder. The 2025 award writes the incentive down: on a change of control operational milestones lapse and market-cap milestones vest, 423.7M shares are 10.7% dilution, the first $2.0T milestone sits 25% above today's capitalisation, against a $9.74B probable charge and $105.82-120.37B unrecognised. Musk has pledged 207.5M shares, 5.2% of the count; three of nine directors carry outside ties — two to SpaceX (Ehrenpreis, Kimbal Musk), one to Redwood Materials, a Tesla supplier — and the committee uses two. [S5, S135, S138]

### Policy is a $5.60 option; competition is a terminal-value risk

Twenty-five state attorneys general and 12 cities and counties sued on 2026-03-19 in the D.C. Circuit over EPA's 2026-02-12 repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding, consolidated on 2026-05-20; a reversal restores the credit pool, but $1.5B of credits at 15x is $22.5B, $5.6 a share, against Q3 credit revenue of $113M, down 73% and 45.8% of FY2025 operating income. Competition is different in kind: BYD holds 2.4% of the European market at EUR 5,500 less per car, Xiaomi is near break-even in its first production year and Waymo runs 500,000 paid rides a week on 4,000 vehicles. If revenue per mile falls from $0.60 to $0.45, the reverse DCF needs 20.9M robotaxis rather than 15.7M, above global annual capacity — $40-60 a share off the bull branch and nothing off 2027 earnings. The unknown unknown is a recall that grounds the fleet and removes its training data. [S136, S138, S59, S4]

## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis

Tesla is two assets inside one ticker: a business worth $43.00 a share on a sum of the parts — vehicles, energy, services and $36.2B of net cash at peer multiples — and an option worth $360.30, or 89% of the $403.30 close, on a robotaxi and humanoid franchise that discloses no revenue. Three tests separate cleanly. The need is real: grid storage is Tesla's fastest-growing equipment market and energy earned a 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026. The capability is partly defensible: 2.5M vehicles of installed capacity, dry-electrode 4680 cells in production on both electrodes since January 2026, and a $34,436 cost per vehicle. The economics do not scale on any evidence available at 2026-10-29: 1,051 authorised robotaxi vehicles in Texas on 2026-10-27, 544 of them Cybercabs, paid driverless rides confined to Austin since 2026-09-03, no disclosed fare, and a reverse DCF that needs $141B of 2031 free cash flow. The outcome at this price is unattractive unless an event rather than operating delivery reprices the option. [S6, S15, S150]

The sell side is almost at the price: the 2026-10-25 consensus is Hold across 48 firms with a $408.61 average target, 1.3% above the close, and the published range runs from $128.11 to $600 — a 4.7x spread that makes consensus an average of incompatible models. We put the core at $43.00 a share on 3,952.6M shares — $170.0B, within $5 of Morgan Stanley's $47 for the same assets — and autonomy at $259B in the base case: 35% × $40B regional, 40% × $126B licensing, 20% × $600B multi-metro, 5% × $1,500B dominance, which is $65.5 a share on the issued count, and the base case is $107. That $259B is 2.1 times the $126B post-money at which Waymo raised $16B in February 2026. [S141, S144, S120]

### Every branch but one sits below the price

The tree puts 25% on a bull case that still loses 47%, because the price sits above it. In the bull case ($212) robotaxi reaches several metros at 1.0x Waymo and energy trades at 6.0x sales, a 12.1% annual loss to 2031. In the base case ($107) the core is valued at peer multiples and autonomy at that $259B blend, a 73% loss; regional-only autonomy, the 35% branch, is $10.1 a share, so a base built on it would be $53 and would average $84 with the same bull and bear outcomes — a $27 difference that does not change the call. In the bear case ($19) autonomy is written down, vehicles trade at GM's implied 0.39x sales and the undisclosed Terafab commitment takes cash, a 95% loss. The weights sum to 100%; the probability-weighted value is $111, 72% below the close. The merger sits outside the tree: adding it as a separate binary at 40% probability and a $454 mid-point lifts expected value to $248, still 38% below the price. That arithmetic is why the call is Reduce and not Sell — the option has value, just not $1,424B of it. [S120, S6]

Assumptions 2 and 3 decide whether the core is worth $43.00 or $21.75, and management can still influence both in 2027 — the ex-credit operating margin has been cut to 2.2-2.5%, while energy and services supplied $1,688M of the $5,494M third-quarter gross profit at a margin 2.5 times Fluence's 13.1%. Assumptions 4 and 5 are about survival and dilution rather than growth: $36.18B of net cash covers eighteen months of zero free cash flow, but not that plus a $16.8B capital call whose Tesla share is undisclosed. | Amazon | cautionary | 1999-2001 | The business compounded into one of the great franchises, but the stock fell more than 90% and took a decade to recover; the option paid only for the holder who could sit through the drawdown. | S143 |

| Waymo | best | 2024-2026 | The valuation went from $45B in October 2024 to $126B in February 2026 on 500,000 paid driverless rides a week — proof the service can scale, and a mark that Tesla's autonomy value exceeds 11-fold. | S120 |

The precedents give one rule: when a real technology shift is already in the price, the entry multiple sets the return, not whether the technology wins; the base rate for a follower in autonomy is a write-off, not a slow fade; and the leader's private mark, $126B, is the only independent price for the option — 9% of what the market pays for Tesla's version. A holder should own Tesla's autonomy at a discount to that mark, not at 11.3 times it, and size the position so the Cruise outcome is survivable. [S140, S142]

### Where the case turns, and what to do now

Below $111 the probability-weighted value supports ownership; between $111 and $250 the buyer is paying for the merger option; above $250 the stock is a binary bet on a committee. At $403.30 it sits in the third zone, with the ten-year Treasury at 4.99% raising the discount rate on post-2030 cash flows. Do not invest new money now. Wait for one of three milestones: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile, a California driverless deployment permit, or special-committee terms at a premium to market rather than at market. If the mandate requires exposure, hold a residual of 0.25-0.5% of net asset value, sized so a failed vote and a 30% drawdown do not breach the risk budget, and vote against any ratio that transfers value to the controlling shareholder. Pass on the blue-sky branch: it needs global robotaxi and humanoid dominance and pays 8% from here. Diligence questions: revenue per vehicle per week in Austin, the share of rides running without a safety driver, and Tesla's share of the Terafab capital call. Confidence is high that the core is not worth $403.30, medium on the autonomy tree, low on the merger. What would change the call: a second consecutive quarter of double-digit ex-credit operating margin, an FSD licensing contract with a named automaker, or a ratio that values Tesla at a premium to its undisturbed price. [S15, S5]

## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis

Tesla offers no cash exit at $1.59 trillion. It has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation, and its entire $45.4B of cash and short-term investments would retire 2.85% of the 3.953B shares outstanding. The largest buyout ever completed — Electronic Arts at $55B in August 2026 — is 3.4% of Tesla's market capitalisation, so no financial sponsor can write this cheque, and no automaker can either: GM and Ford together are $118.4B, 7.4% of Tesla. What remains is a sale into a market that trades $14.0B of Tesla a day, or a share exchange into SpaceX, and both leave the return hostage to a re-rating that five years have not delivered. [S3, S130]

### The company returns nothing, and cannot return much

Tesla's 10-K states that it has never declared or paid a cash dividend, does not anticipate doing so, and purchased no equity securities in fiscal 2025. Trailing free cash flow of $3,303M is a 0.2% yield on the capitalisation, and nine-month capital expenditure of $13,014M runs at 2.1x depreciation: the cash is going into factories, cells and training compute, not to holders. Against GM's 12.4% total shareholder yield and Ford's 5.9%, Tesla's is zero. Even a maximal buyback using the whole cash pile would move the share count by less than three points, and it would leave a company spending $17B a year on capital projects with no liquidity buffer. Capital return is a governance choice, and the controlling shareholder has consistently chosen reinvestment. [S6]

### The exit that always works is the tape

The secondary market is the only channel that is always open. Tesla trades 36.96M shares and $14.0B a day over twenty days, so a $500M position is 3.6% of a single day's value and no holder is trapped by liquidity. Short interest of 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float and 2.2 days to cover, means the marginal seller is not fighting a crowded short either. Passive ownership is a flow that follows the index and the price rather than a bid that supports it; Tesla's exact float-adjusted S&P 500 weight is not disclosed in the sources retrieved, and after the top ten names reached 39.03% of the index on 2026-10-10 the marginal index buyer is a shrinking share of demand. [S15, S114]

### No control buyer exists, at any price

A cash takeover is arithmetically out of reach. The pieces themselves are worth $170B on the sum of the parts — vehicles at 1.0x sales, energy at 3.5x, net cash at book — and a control buyer for those assets alone would pay $200-250B with a premium, which is one-eighth of the current capitalisation and therefore not a route to today's price. Alphabet, at $3,493.5B, is the only US company with the balance sheet to write a $1.6T cheque, and it is the closest competitor in autonomous driving, which makes antitrust the binding constraint rather than price. Musk's 19.8% stake and 207.5M pledged shares mean nothing happens without him, and a hostile approach is legally and financially impossible at this size. [S5, S6]

### The one live route is a share exchange with SpaceX

On 2026-10-21 both boards formed special committees to explore a combination, days after Musk called the idea a "good idea" on the third-quarter earnings call. SpaceX listed on 2026-06-12 at $135 a share and a $1.77T valuation, reached $2.1T on its first day, and the combined group would be worth well over $3 trillion. At those marks Tesla holders would own 43% of the equity — but they would exchange one-share-one-vote stock for a company where super-voting shares give Musk about 84% of the vote, against 20% at Tesla. That is the governance price of the only transformative exit available, and it is being negotiated by two boards that have not historically pushed back: Tesla invested $2B in xAI after its chair expressed scepticism, and it rescued SolarCity in 2016.
